_readme: Vocabulary the speech engine gets wrong, and what it should have said.
HOW TO ADD A TERM: add an object to `terms` with the canonical spelling and
the wrong things you have actually heard it produce. Save the file — the
server re-reads it when the mtime changes, so no restart is needed.
`heard` entries are matched literally (case- and punctuation-insensitive) and
may span several words, which is the point: the engine breaks words in the
wrong places, so 'a Lexus' has to be matched as one thing to become 'Alexa'.
Anything NOT listed can still be caught by sound-alike matching, but only when
the pronunciation is distinctive enough to be safe (see `minPhoneticLength` in
server.js). Short words collide far too easily — 'cold', 'called' and 'clot'
all sound exactly like 'Claude' to the matcher — so short terms are corrected
ONLY from this list. That is deliberate: a wrong correction is worse than a
missed one, because this text becomes instructions an agent acts on.
`protect` is the last line of defence: ordinary words that must never be
rewritten by sound-alike matching, whatever it thinks.

heard: c l o u d e u
terms.note: The worst offender — three messages in a row failed on this one, including a spelled-out attempt. 'cloud' is listed knowingly: this user says 'Claude' constantly and bare 'cloud' almost never; the common collocations ('the cloud', 'cloud storage', 'cloud nine') are protected below, and the longer 'Cloudflare' wins the match ahead of it. 'clawed', 'cloudy' and 'clod' were tried and REMOVED — they are ordinary words, and rewriting 'he clawed at the door' is exactly the kind of mistake that costs more trust than the fix is worth. If bare 'cloud' ever bites, delete it from this list.
Longer spans are matched first, so this beats 'cloud' -> 'Claude'.

Broken across a word boundary every time, and never phonetically close enough to catch by sound alone. The 'to belt' variants came from round-tripping through piper rather than from the user; they are nonsense phrases, so listing them costs nothing.

The worst term in this file after 'Claude', and the only one the phonetic pass cannot help with at all: the engine loses the leading v- in nearly every miss, so 'Bacunya' and 'Vikunja' are nowhere near each other by sound and this exact list is the ONLY thing that catches them. Everything after the original seven was read back out of the relay record rather than guessed, and every one is a word he actually dictated: 'KoongJub' (08-08, 'getting that the KoongJub MCP running', one minute after Vikunja was named in the same tab), 'Baccuna' (08-27), 'kunea' + 'Kunia' + 'Vaccunia' (08-28), 'Kuna' (08-29), 'Bacunya' + 'Bacunia' + 'buckoonia' + 'Koenja' (09-01, four different non-words in one session, the last two inside the very sentence asking for this fix). 'bakunya', 'buccoonia' and the three split spans are NOT separately observed - they are alternate spellings and word-breaks of sounds that were, and they cost nothing because none of them is an English word or phrase. TWO THINGS WERE DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT. 'koenja thing' was listed briefly and REMOVED: a span ending in an ordinary word swallows it, so 'that Koenja thing needs doing' came out as 'that Vikunja needs doing' - a word silently deleted from an instruction an agent then acts on, which is the exact failure this file exists to prevent. Bare 'koenja' already catches it and keeps the noun. Lowercase 'vikunja' was left out because it does nothing: loadTerms() drops a heard form that differs from its term only by case, and `canonical` then claims the span - so the capitalisation-only entries this file documents for MCP, Docker and GitHub have never once fired. That is a matcher bug, not a vocabulary bug; tracked as Vikunja #147 and deliberately not fixed here. Bare 'kuna' IS listed, knowingly, the way bare 'cloud' is: it is not English, but it is one consonant away from 'tuna'. If it ever rewrites a sandwich, delete that one entry.
Lowercase 'mcp' is corrected for capitalisation only.

Deliberately empty. The device name is indistinguishable from the ordinary word, and rewriting 'echo' would be wrong far more often than right. Listed so the decision is visible rather than forgotten.
'coordinate her' was deliberately NOT listed — 'coordinate her schedule' is a perfectly ordinary sentence.
Capitalisation only. 'doctor' is NOT listed — it is a common word and the cost of getting it wrong is far higher than the cost of fixing it by hand.
Empty on purpose: 'whisper' is an ordinary English word and the engine gets it right anyway.
The speech protocol, capitalised like the project.
